desc:
You stand on some index of the array a and make a series of jumps, always to the right. The jumps are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... and alternate between two kinds. From index i:

  • on an odd-numbered jump you go to the index j > i with the smallest value a[j] ≥ a[i];
  • on an even-numbered jump you go to the index j > i with the largest value a[j] ≤ a[i].

If several indices have that best value, take the smallest index among them. If no index qualifies, you are stuck. A starting index is good if some series of jumps (there is only one, since every jump is forced) reaches the last index. The last index itself is always good.

Return the number of good starting indices.

Example 1

a = [10,13,12,14,15]
Output: 2
From index 3 (value 14) the first jump goes to 15 at the end. From index 0: jump 1 goes to 12, jump 2 needs a value ≤ 12 to the right of it and finds none, so it is stuck. Indices 1 and 2 get stuck the same way. Good starts: indices 3 and 4.

Example 2

a = [2,3,1,1,4]
Output: 3
Good starts: indices 1, 3 and 4. For example from index 3 (value 1): jump 1 goes to 4, the last index. From index 0 (value 2): jump 1 goes to 3 (index 1), jump 2 goes to the largest value ≤ 3 on the right, which is 1 at index 2 (the first of two ones), jump 3 goes to the smallest value ≥ 1, which is 1 at index 3, jump 4 needs a value ≤ 1 to the right of index 3 and finds none, so it is stuck.

Example 3

a = [5]
Output: 1
hints: Simulating every start for as long as it takes is O(n) jumps per start, O(n2) overall. Notice that a jump from index i only depends on i and the kind of jump, not on how you got there.

Let up[i] mean 'standing on i and the next jump is odd, can I reach the end?' and down[i] the same for an even next jump. Then up[i] = down[j] where j is the odd-jump target, and down[i] = up[j'] for the even-jump target j'.

Compute the answers from right to left. Keep the already seen indices to the right of i in a sorted structure of pairs (value, index); the odd target is the first pair not smaller than (a[i], -1) and the even target is found by taking the last pair with value ≤ a[i] and then moving to the smallest index of that value. Count the indices with up[i] true.
editorial: Every jump is forced, so a start is good or bad independent of how the walk got there. Define up[i] (the next jump from i is odd) and down[i] (the next jump is even) as 'the last index is reachable'. The last index has both set. For i from right to left, find the odd target j (the successor of a[i] among the values to the right, ties to the smallest index) and the even target j' (the floor of a[i], ties again to the smallest index), then up[i] = down[j] and down[i] = up[j'], treating a missing target as false. The answer is the number of true up[i]: every start begins with jump number 1, an odd jump.

The only data structure needed is an ordered set of (value, index) pairs that supports insert, successor and floor, exactly what a balanced BST offers. In Python a sorted list with bisect and insort plays that role: inserting is a fast memmove and the queries are binary searches. Total O(n log n) comparisons (O(n2) tiny memmove work in the worst case, fine for n = 5,000). A monotonic-stack solution over the values sorted by (value, index) also exists.
solution:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort


def countGoodStarts(a):
    n = len(a)
    up = [False] * n
    down = [False] * n
    up[n - 1] = down[n - 1] = True
    seen = [(a[n - 1], n - 1)]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        v = a[i]
        k = bisect_left(seen, (v, -1))
        if k < len(seen):
            up[i] = down[seen[k][1]]
        k = bisect_right(seen, (v, n + 1)) - 1
        if k >= 0:
            k = bisect_left(seen, (seen[k][0], -1))
            down[i] = up[seen[k][1]]
        insort(seen, (v, i))
    return sum(up)
